summary.text: Decompose the recurrence as \(a_n=u_n+v_n\), where \(u_{n+2}=64u_n\) gives \(u_{2n+1}=32\cdot64^n\), while \(v_{n+2}=-4v_{n+1}-64v_n\). An inductively established addition formula for a companion sequence yields \(v_{2n+1}=4v_n^2-32\cdot64^n\), so the exponential terms cancel and \(a_{2n+1}=(2v_n)^2\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n.
\]
We prove the stronger explicit assertion
\[
 a_{2n+1}=(2v_n)^2
\]
for a suitable auxiliary integer sequence \((v_n)\). This immediately implies that every odd-indexed term is a perfect square.

Define two integer sequences \((u_n)\) and \((v_n)\) by
\[
u_0=0,\qquad u_1=32,\qquad u_{n+2}=64u_n,
\]
and
\[
v_0=-1,\qquad v_1=-28,\qquad
v_{n+2}=-4v_{n+1}-64v_n.
\]

We first show that
\[
 a_n=u_n+v_n\qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{1}
\]
For the first four indices, the required values are obtained directly from the definitions. Indeed,
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
n&0&1&2&3\\ \hline
u_n&0&32&0&2048\\
v_n&-1&-28&176&1088
\end{array}
\]
because
\[
v_2=-4(-28)-64(-1)=176
\]
and
\[
v_3=-4(176)-64(-28)=1088.
\]
Thus the sums \(u_n+v_n\) for \(n=0,1,2,3\) are respectively
\[
-1,\ 4,\ 176,\ 3136,
\]
which are the initial values of \(a_n\).

It remains to check that \(u_n+v_n\) obeys the same fourth-order recurrence as \(a_n\). For \(u\), the recurrence \(u_{r+2}=64u_r\) gives
\[
u_{n+4}=64u_{n+2}=4096u_n.
\]
It also gives \(u_{n+3}=64u_{n+1}\), so
\[
-4u_{n+3}+256u_{n+1}+4096u_n
=-4(64u_{n+1})+256u_{n+1}+4096u_n
=4096u_n=u_{n+4}.
\]
For \(v\), applying its recurrence twice gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_{n+4}
&=-4v_{n+3}-64v_{n+2}\\
&=-4v_{n+3}-64(-4v_{n+1}-64v_n)\\
&=-4v_{n+3}+256v_{n+1}+4096v_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently \(u+v\) satisfies the fourth-order recurrence of \(a\). Since it also has the same four initial values, induction on the index proves (1).

The odd-indexed terms of \(u\) are particularly simple:
\[
 u_{2n+1}=32\cdot 64^n. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, this is true at \(n=0\), since \(u_1=32\). If it holds for \(n\), then
\[
u_{2(n+1)+1}=u_{2n+3}=64u_{2n+1}
=64\bigl(32\cdot64^n\bigr)=32\cdot64^{n+1}.
\]

We next derive the corresponding formula for the odd-indexed terms of \(v\). Introduce another sequence \((w_n)\) by
\[
w_0=2,\qquad w_1=-4,\qquad
w_{n+2}=-4w_{n+1}-64w_n. \tag{3}
\]
Thus \(w\) satisfies the same second-order recurrence as \(v\), but with different initial values.

The key identity for \(w\) is the following addition formula: for all nonnegative integers \(m,k\),
\[
 w_{k+2m}+64^m w_k=w_{k+m}w_m. \tag{4}
\]
We prove (4) by induction on \(m\), in a form valid simultaneously for every \(k\).

For \(m=0\), its left side is
\[
w_k+64^0w_k=2w_k,
\]
and its right side is \(w_kw_0=2w_k\), since \(w_0=2\).

For \(m=1\), recurrence (3) says
\[
w_{k+2}+64w_k=-4w_{k+1}=w_{k+1}w_1,
\]
which is exactly (4).

Now suppose the identity is known for \(m\) and for \(m+1\), at every value of the second parameter \(k\). We prove it for \(m+2\). Apply the induction hypothesis for \(m+1\) with \(k+1\) in place of \(k\). This yields
\[
w_{k+2m+3}+64^{m+1}w_{k+1}
=w_{k+m+2}w_{m+1},
\]
and hence
\[
w_{k+2m+3}
=w_{k+m+2}w_{m+1}-64^{m+1}w_{k+1}. \tag{5}
\]
Apply the induction hypothesis for \(m\) with \(k+2\) in place of \(k\). It yields
\[
w_{k+2m+2}+64^m w_{k+2}=w_{k+m+2}w_m,
\]
so
\[
w_{k+2m+2}
=w_{k+m+2}w_m-64^m w_{k+2}. \tag{6}
\]
Using the recurrence for \(w_{k+2m+4}\), followed by (5) and (6), we now obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
&w_{k+2m+4}+64^{m+2}w_k\\
&=-4w_{k+2m+3}-64w_{k+2m+2}+64^{m+2}w_k\\
&=-4\bigl(w_{k+m+2}w_{m+1}-64^{m+1}w_{k+1}\bigr)\\
&\quad-64\bigl(w_{k+m+2}w_m-64^m w_{k+2}\bigr)
   +64^{m+2}w_k\\
&=w_{k+m+2}(-4w_{m+1}-64w_m)\\
&\quad+64^{m+1}\bigl(4w_{k+1}+w_{k+2}+64w_k\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
By recurrence (3),
\[
-4w_{m+1}-64w_m=w_{m+2},
\]
while
\[
4w_{k+1}+w_{k+2}+64w_k=0.
\]
Therefore the last displayed expression is simply
\[
w_{k+m+2}w_{m+2}.
\]
This is precisely (4) with \(m+2\) in place of \(m\). The two base cases and this two-step induction prove (4) for every \(m,k\ge 0\).

We now relate \(w\) to \(v\). We claim that
\[
 w_{n+1}=4v_n\qquad(n\ge 0). \tag{7}
\]
At \(n=0\), this reads \(w_1=-4=4(-1)=4v_0\). At \(n=1\),
\[
w_2=-4w_1-64w_0=16-128=-112=4(-28)=4v_1.
\]
Thereafter both sides satisfy the same recurrence: if (7) holds at \(n\) and \(n+1\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_{n+3}
&=-4w_{n+2}-64w_{n+1}\\
&=-4(4v_{n+1})-64(4v_n)\\
&=4(-4v_{n+1}-64v_n)=4v_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus (7) follows by induction.

Specialize the addition formula (4) to \(k=0\) and \(m=n+1\). Since \(w_0=2\), it gives
\[
 w_{2n+2}+2\cdot64^{n+1}=w_{n+1}^2. \tag{8}
\]
Using (7), first with index \(2n+1\) and then with index \(n\), equation (8) becomes
\[
4v_{2n+1}+2\cdot64^{n+1}=(4v_n)^2=16v_n^2.
\]
As \(64^{n+1}=64\cdot64^n\), division by \(4\) gives the duplication formula
\[
 v_{2n+1}=4v_n^2-32\cdot64^n. \tag{9}
\]

Finally, combine (1), (2), and (9):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2n+1}
&=u_{2n+1}+v_{2n+1}\\
&=32\cdot64^n+\bigl(4v_n^2-32\cdot64^n\bigr)\\
&=4v_n^2=(2v_n)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus for every nonnegative integer \(n\), the odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is the square of the integer \(2v_n\). Hence \(a(2n+1)\) is a perfect square for all \(n\ge 0\), as claimed.
